item.prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: By the time the bus pulled into the parking lot, the first bell had already sounded, so Marco hurried to class.

item.correct_answer: By the time the bus pulled into the parking lot, the first bell had already sounded, so Marco hurried to class.
error_sites: past perfect 'had already sounded' for the action finished before the bus arrived

student_error.By the time the bus pulled into the park: uses simple past for the earlier action, not seeing that 'By the time ... pulled in' calls for 'had sounded'

does not track time across the sentence: misses the past perfect and also drifts into present tense at the end

choices: Although the art room was crowded after lunch, the students kept painting, and Ms. Lee walked between the tables to help.
Although the art room was crowded after lunch, but the students kept painting, and Ms. Lee walked between the tables to help.
Although the art room was crowded after lunch, the students kept painting, Ms. Lee walked between the tables to help.
Although the art room was crowded after lunch, but the students kept painting, Ms. Lee walked between the tables to help.
item.correct_answer: Although the art room was crowded after lunch, the students kept painting, and Ms. Lee walked between the tables to help.
error_sites: no 'but' after a clause that begins with 'Although'
the conjunction 'and' joining the last two independent clauses

student_error.Although the art room was crowded after: adds 'but' because the idea is a contrast, not seeing that 'Although' already supplies it
joins two complete sentences with only a comma
joins clauses by feel: doubles up the contrast word and leaves the last two clauses with only a comma

item.explanation: 'Although' already links the first clause to 'the students kept painting', so adding 'but' is a second connector. 'Ms. Lee walked ...' is a complete sentence, so it needs 'and' after the comma; a comma alone makes a comma splice.
item.varied_dimension: extra 'but' after an 'Although' clause; missing conjunction between the last two clauses (comma splice)

rated_no.option: Although the art room was crowded after lunch, but the students kept painting, Ms. Lee walked between the tables to help.
reasons: two errors look off
stacked errors read badly

item.prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: Ms. Ford let us write either a poem or draw a comic, and she wanted both a title and a date.

Ms. Ford let us either write a poem or draw a comic, and she wanted both a title and a date.
Ms. Ford let us write either a poem or draw a comic, and she wanted both a title but also a date.
item.correct_answer: Ms. Ford let us either write a poem or draw a comic, and she wanted both a title and a date.
error_sites: 'either' placed before the verb 'write' to match 'or draw'

student_error.Ms. Ford let us write either a poem or d: puts 'either' before 'a poem' so it is set against the verb phrase 'draw a comic'
student_error.Ms. Ford let us either write a poem or d: mixes up 'both ... and' with 'not only ... but also'
student_error.Ms. Ford let us write either a poem or d: does not know how correlative pairs work: misplaces 'either' and borrows 'but also' for 'both'

item.explanation: 'Either' and 'or' must come before matching parts: 'either write a poem or draw a comic' (two verbs). 'Both' pairs only with 'and'; 'but also' belongs with 'not only'.
item.varied_dimension: placement of 'either' so both halves match; the partner word for 'both'

rated_no.option: Ms. Ford let us either write a poem or draw a comic, and she wanted both a title but also a date.
reasons: "both...but also" sounds wrong

item.correct_answer: Mr. Hale split the leftover clay between Dev and me, so Dev and I could finish our sculptures before the art show.
error_sites: objective 'me' as an object of the preposition 'between'
subjective 'I' in the compound subject 'Dev and I'

student_error.Mr. Hale split the leftover clay between: uses 'I' after 'between' because 'Dev and I' sounds more correct
uses 'me' in the compound subject, which sounds natural in speech
chooses by sound instead of job in the sentence, so the two cases end up swapped

item.explanation: 'Between' is a preposition, so its objects take the objective case: 'between Dev and me'. 'Dev and I' is the subject of 'could finish', so it takes the subjective 'I'. Test by dropping 'Dev': 'between me', 'I could finish'.
item.varied_dimension: objective case after the preposition 'between'; subjective case in a compound subject

rated_no.option: Mr. Hale split the leftover clay between Dev and I, so Dev and me could finish our sculptures before the art show.
reasons: two errors make it inconsistent and odd

item.map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
item.prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: The twins built the birdhouse theirselves, but their uncle cut the roof pieces himself because the saw was too dangerous for them.
The twins built the birdhouse themselves, but their uncle cut the roof pieces hisself because the saw was too dangerous for them.
The twins built the birdhouse theirselves, but their uncle cut the roof pieces hisself because the saw was too dangerous for them.
The twins built the birdhouse themselves, but their uncle cut the roof pieces himself because the saw was too dangerous for them.
item.correct_answer: The twins built the birdhouse themselves, but their uncle cut the roof pieces himself because the saw was too dangerous for them.

student_error.The twins built the birdhouse theirselve: builds the plural intensive on 'their', like 'myself' and 'yourself'
student_error.The twins built the birdhouse themselves: builds the singular intensive on 'his', like 'myself' and 'yourself'
student_error.The twins built the birdhouse theirselve: forms intensive pronouns from possessives ('my-self', so 'their-selves', 'his-self') in both places

item.explanation: The standard intensive pronouns are 'themselves' and 'himself'. 'Theirselves' and 'hisself' are nonstandard forms made by analogy with 'myself' and 'yourself'.
item.varied_dimension: standard plural intensive pronoun; standard singular intensive pronoun

rated_no.option: The twins built the birdhouse theirselves, but their uncle cut the roof pieces hisself because the saw was too dangerous for them.
reasons: two nonstandard forms stand out

plural 'them' for the same antecedent, later in the clause

student_error.We planted tomato seedlings in April, an: shifts to singular 'it', thinking of the garden as one thing

rated_no.option: We planted tomato seedlings in April, and by July the plants were so tall that it needed stakes to hold it up.
reasons: two mismatches stand out
two pronoun errors read badly

item.prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: The mayor herself presented the science award to Eli and me, and afterward Eli and I thanked her for visiting.

The mayor herself presented the science award to Eli and me, and afterward Eli and myself thanked her for visiting.
The mayor herself presented the science award to Eli and myself, and afterward Eli and myself thanked her for visiting.
item.correct_answer: The mayor herself presented the science award to Eli and me, and afterward Eli and I thanked her for visiting.
error_sites: subject pronoun 'I' in the compound subject (not 'myself')

student_error.The mayor herself presented the science: uses 'myself' as the object because it sounds more polite than 'me'
uses 'myself' as part of the subject to avoid choosing between 'I' and 'me'
treats 'myself' as a polite all-purpose pronoun in both places

item.explanation: 'Herself' is correct as an intensive for 'The mayor'. But '-self' pronouns cannot stand in for ordinary ones: 'to Eli and me' (object of 'to') and 'Eli and I thanked her' (subject). Nothing in the sentence makes 'myself' refer back to an 'I' already in its clause.
item.varied_dimension: object pronoun vs reflexive after a preposition in a compound; subject pronoun vs reflexive in a compound subject

rated_no.option: The mayor herself presented the science award to Eli and myself, and afterward Eli and myself thanked her for visiting.
reasons: two errors stand out

item.correct_answer: In music class we practiced a song called “The Night Is Ours to Keep,” which has a tricky high note.
error_sites: the short verb 'Is' inside the title

student_error.In music class we practiced a song calle: lowercases 'is' because it is a short word, like 'to'
lowercases 'ours' because pronouns seem like minor words

item.explanation: In a title, verbs and pronouns are capitalized however short they are: 'Is', 'Ours'. Only articles, short prepositions and conjunctions, and the 'to' of an infinitive stay lowercase.
item.cap_rule: titles of works: a short verb and a pronoun inside the title are capitalized, while small words like 'to' stay lowercase

rated_no.option: In music class we practiced a song called “The Night Is ours to Keep,” which has a tricky high note.
reasons: lowercasing "ours" but not "Is" looks inconsistent
